extracted.intended_audience: employers, HR professionals, labor lawyers, and stakeholders subject to the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Defines the two-pronged "senior executive" exception to the FTC non-compete rule by specifying a compensation threshold and a job-duties (policy-making) test, plus attendant definitional and administrability rules for applying the exception to existing non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-pronged definition of "senior executive"
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §910.1, a senior executive is a worker who was in a policy-making position and who received from a person for the employment total annual compensation of at least $151,164 in the preceding year (or the annualized equivalents for part-year employment or prior-year departure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies only where both the job-duties prong (policy-making position / authority) and the compensation threshold are met; paragraph (2)(ii) covers part-year policy-making service (hired/promoted/demoted during the preceding year) and paragraph (2)(iii) covers workers who departed prior to the preceding year (uses the year prior to departure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation threshold amount: $151,164
rubrics_metrics.description: The compensation threshold for the senior executive exception is $151,164 in total annual compensation, based on the 85th percentile of earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally (2023 data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chosen to isolate highly compensated individuals likely to have bespoke, negotiated non-competes and to be less likely to experience coercion/exploitation; intended to be administrable and align with DOL/IRS familiar thresholds. Not adjusted for locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of annualized compensation for part-year employment or pre-departure year
rubrics_metrics.description: If the worker was employed during only part of the preceding year or departed prior to the preceding year, total compensation is annualized to determine whether it meets the $151,164 threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (2)(ii) and (2)(iii) implement annualization so hires, departures, promotions/demotions, or departed workers with multi‑year non-competes are captured appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total annual compensation — included components
rubrics_metrics.description: Total annual compensation may include salary, commissions, nondiscretionary bonuses and other nondiscretionary compensation earned during that 52‑week period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nondiscretionary bonuses/compensation includes amounts paid pursuant to any prior contract, agreement, or promise, including performance bonuses the worker knows and can expect. The definition follows DOL 29 CFR 541.601(b)(1) as to types of compensation that can count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total annual compensation — excluded components
rubrics_metrics.description: Total annual compensation does not include board, lodging and other facilities as defined in 29 CFR 541.606, and does not include payments for medical insurance, payments for life insurance, contributions to retirement plans, and the cost of other similar fringe benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirrors DOL/29 CFR cross-referenced exclusions; consult 29 CFR 531.32 and 541.606 for details on 'other facilities' and related wage-payment rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: No base-salary minimum requirement for total annual compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the DOL highly compensated employee test, the FTC definition does not require a base salary portion of total annual compensation; compensation can be structured in varied ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: senior-executive pay often uses variable/vested compensation (e.g., CEOs with $1 salary); rule allows nondiscretionary forms without mandating a salary floor to qualify as total annual compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "preceding year" (employer choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'preceding year' allows a person's choice among: the most recent 52‑week year, the most recent calendar year, the most recent fiscal year, or the most recent anniversary of hire year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives employers flexibility to use the period for which compensation data are most readily available; mirrors DOL approach (if not identified in advance, calendar year applies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing compensation threshold with job duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule pairs the $151,164 compensation threshold with a job-duties (policy-making) test to identify senior executives eligible for the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination is intended to reduce 'cliff effects' and avoid excluding or inappropriately including workers; the compensation threshold alone was rejected as an insufficient screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: No locality adjustment to the compensation threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission declines to adopt geographic or locality adjustments and adopts a uniform national compensation threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: locality adjustments would be administratively burdensome and confusing, would not resolve intra-state urban/rural variation, and would be difficult in cross-border/remote work environments; neither DOL nor IRS uses geographic variation for their comparable thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of alternative compensation thresholds and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considered—and rejected—various alternatives (e.g., $100,000, DOL's $107,432, $330,000 IRS limit, state/local thresholds, percentage-of‑employer-top-10% rules, local median wage multiples, annual inflation adjustments) for qualifying senior executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for rejection include over-/under-inclusiveness, administrative complexity, unpredictability for employers/workers, geographic and firm-size disparities, and incompatibility with the exception's goals (targeting bespoke negotiated non-competes and avoiding coercion). The rule explains why each alternative was deemed inferior to $151,164 plus duties test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "policy-making position"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Policy-making position" is defined as a business entity's president, chief executive officer or the equivalent; any other officer of a business entity who has policy-making authority; or any other natural person who has policy-making authority for the business entity similar to an officer with policy-making authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes officers of subsidiaries/affiliates who have policy-making authority for the common enterprise; excludes persons who do not have policy-making authority over the common enterprise as a whole. Presidents/CEOs and equivalents are presumed senior executives (no need to assess further).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "officer" (adopted from SEC 17 CFR 240.3b-2)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Officer" is defined as a president, vice president, secretary, treasurer or principal financial officer, comptroller or principal accounting officer, and any natural person routinely performing corresponding functions for any business entity (incorporated or unincorporated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission adopts the SEC's wording to maintain consistency and rely on SEC expertise; the definition's inclusion of equivalent roles accounts for variation in job titles across entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "policy-making authority"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Policy-making authority" is final authority to make policy decisions that control significant aspects of a business entity or a common enterprise and does not include authority limited to advising or exerting influence over such policy decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on final decision-making power that controls significant aspects of the organization; excludes mere advisors or those whose decisions are limited to a segment that does not control significant aspects of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional (duties-based) test rather than title-only
rubrics_metrics.description: The job-duties test focuses primarily on actual job duties and authority rather than formal job titles because titles vary and may not reflect real authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to avoid overinclusion from title inflation and ensure the test isolates workers who truly have bargaining power and bespoke agreements; employers must assess functional authority when applying the duties prong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of policy-making authority at the business-as-a-whole level
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy-making authority is assessed based on the authority a worker has to make policy decisions that control significant aspects of the business entity as a whole, not authority limited to a department, office, or subsidiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department heads or division managers who only control decisions within a subunit normally will not qualify; examples include heads of marketing divisions or hospital surgery practice heads who lack enterprise-wide policy authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common enterprise concept and criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine when subsidiary/affiliate executives may be treated as having enterprise-wide authority, the Commission defines 'common enterprise' by indicators such as maintaining officers/directors/workers in common, operating under common control, sharing offices, commingling funds, and sharing advertising/marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If entities form a common enterprise (integrated business entities), authority must be assessed with respect to the common enterprise; otherwise, executives of separate subsidiaries/affiliates may qualify if they have policy-making authority over that subsidiary/affiliate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion to prevent corporate-structure evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives who have policy-making authority only over a subsidiary or affiliate of a common enterprise, but not over the common enterprise as a whole, are excluded from the definition of senior executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to prevent businesses from structuring entities to manufacture senior-executive status; only individuals with authority over the common enterprise as a whole can qualify in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of senior-executive status for presidents and chief executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents, chief executive officers, and their equivalents are presumed to be senior executives—employers need not separately show policy-making authority for these roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption simplifies application for the highest-level titles, recognizing that such roles typically possess enterprise‑level policy-making authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application limited to existing non-competes (one-time exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The senior executive exception applies only to existing non-competes (i.e., it's a one-time exemption for previously executed non-compete agreements), so the Commission declined to adopt inflation updates for the threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the exception is limited to existing non-competes, the threshold need not be indexed for inflation for ongoing application; this narrows the operational impact of the threshold over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on DOL/IRS practices to improve administrability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission aligns its compensation definitions and threshold rationale with DOL and IRS approaches (e.g., types of compensation counted, percentile benchmarking) to reduce compliance burdens on employers familiar with those regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alignment helps employers use existing payroll and reporting practices; the Commission borrowed DOL's definitions for types of compensable items while omitting DOL's base-salary requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of nondiscretionary contractual bonuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance bonuses or other nondiscretionary compensation paid pursuant to any prior contract, agreement, or promise are creditable to total annual compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worker's knowledge and expectation of such bonuses factor into their being nondiscretionary; entire amounts may be credited, increasing likelihood that senior executives nationwide meet the threshold.
